paper_title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

sections.content: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. On real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website. 1. Introduction Robot manipulation policies have progressed from small task-specific networks trained with reinforcement or imitation learning [14, 26, 51, 71] to vision-language-action (VLA) models [1, 3, 22, 35] and world-action models (WAMs) [7, 25, 27], yet all remain data-hungry: they need 1 large teleoperation corpora for each robot and benchmark, and transfer poorly beyond them. Frontier multimodal LLMs offer training-free alternative and can now control robots directly [32, 56, 64, 69], but current agents sit at one of two extremes. Step-wise agents [56, 64, 69] issue one small step per model call, so every step costs seconds of latency and money, and errors compound. Code-as-policy agents [19, 40, 55] instead generate programs over primitive library, which becomes bottleneck: uncovered tasks require new primitives, written by hand or searched offline [19, 39], and feedback arrives only when the program returns, too late to correct failed step. This raises key question: what action granularity is appropriate for an agent policy? We compress 57,534 successful DROID episodes [34] into end-effector keyposes joined by straight lines (Fig. 1b), and find that over 91% of the travel lies on segments longer than 5 cm, and that grasp or release needs only 6 keyposes instead of 96 recorded actions. We therefore hypothesize that, for an agent policy, sequence of sparse end-effector keyposes suffices for manipulation, in place of dense stream of actions. We present SOLVE, training-free framework in which multimodal LLM agent writes sparse, ordered end-effector keyposes, and motion planner [57] executes straight-line motions between them (Fig. 1c). Each keypose is an absolute 6-DoF grasp-point pose with gripper command; one call specifies up to five keyposes, roughly one primitive such as approach, grasp, and lift, and the gripper actuates only upon arrival. The agent decides how many keyposes to use, how far apart, and how fast: single keypose for long free-space motion, and short, slow ones near contact. After each sequence, the agent inspects the outcome before predicting the next one, so visual feedback enters its reasoning at every primitive rather than only at the checks program anticipates. Because each sparse keypose is an absolute commitment, it must be metrically accurate. SOLVE therefore grounds keyposes through sparse metric queries: the agent specifies the few pixels on which its next keypose depends, and tool returns their 3D positions, each annotated with its measurement modality. In RoboDojo and RoboLab simulation, which provide no stereo cameras, the tool triangulates each queried pixel across multiple views by epipolar matching, and falls back to monocular depth estimated by Depth Anything 3 [42], scaled by the known table height, when no multi-view match is found; on the real robot, it directly uses depth from FoundationStereo [58] on stereo infrared camera. Over multiple rounds of keypose reasoning, the agent adapts to the resulting depth noise by itself. On difficult tasks, the agent further improves from its own execution feedback without training: it reflects on rollouts from layouts disjoint from evaluation, and consolidates the notes from several rounds into at most five bounded rules per task, which are provided to it at test time. Since no component of SOLVE is trained, and keyposes live in end-effector space while the planner resolves embodiment-specific execution, the same agent deploys on different robots without modification. SOLVE achieves 74.5% on the dual-arm RoboDojo under the leaderboards metric (Tab. 1) and 84.5% on the single-arm Franka RoboLab [63]. On real UR12e, it completes 75 of 85 episodes across 16 challenging zero-shot tasks (Tab. 4), including table cleaning, peg-in-hole, sketch drawing, and playing Gomoku against human. It does so at $1.7 per episode on average, with one quarter of the model calls and 12 lower cost than step-wise agent (Fig. 1d). Our contributions are as follows: We show that teleoperated demonstrations compress into small number of keyposes and, building on this finding, propose SOLVE, framework in which an LLM agent writes sparse, ordered keyposes for direct manipulation. We propose sparse metric queries, combining cross-view epipolar matching with depth estimation to ground keyposes accurately and efficiently in 3D from RGB in simulation, and use stereo depth on the real robot. We enable the agent to improve from rollouts, and show that SOLVE transfers without modification across robots and benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on RoboDojo, RoboLab, and real robot at 12 lower cost. 2. Related Work End-to-end policies. Vision-language-action (VLA) models [15, 20, 22, 35, 36, 44, 48, 50, 53, 59, 72] and imitation policies that predict action chunks [14, 71] are trained on large teleoperation corpora to emit dense, high-frequency actions; recent work improves their spatial representations [50, 62, 73] and action tokenization [49]. World-action models (WAMs) [68, 17, 25, 27, 31, 37, 38, 41, 46, 60, 66, 74] additionally learn from video to predict future observations and derive actions from them. On RoboDojo [12], the best entries of both families reach 35% on the leaderboard and at most 23% on the Open dimension, whose tasks come without demonstrations. SOLVE instead acts through sparse keyposes and requires no robot-specific training. Agentic policies. growing line of work builds policies around frontier LLMs with little or no training. Codeas-policy methods let the model write programs over perception and control primitives [40]; recent systems benchmark coding agents [18], structure programs as graphs rehearsed in simulation [9], grow skill libraries by evolutionary search [45], or rewrite the training code of neural policies [61]. Agent as Policy [32] similarly writes programs at test time on real arm. Harness methods wrap model with tools, memory and recovery logic, steering frozen VLA as retryable or interruptible tool [10, 15, 70] or calling semantic tools such as grasp and align [43]. Finally, some works Figure 2. Overview of SOLVE. At each call, the multimodal LLM agent queries few pixels, which return depth through epipolar matching across cameras or monocular depth estimation, and writes an ordered sequence of several absolute keyposes that an executor follows along straight lines. Offline, the agent reflects on its own rollouts, and the lessons are merged into general rules for self-improvement. use the model directly as policy, issuing one end-effector target per call [56, 69], several absolute poses each executed for single control step [64], discrete motion units of few centimeters [13], or batches of relative, axis-aligned motion commands. SOLVE is direct policy in that every call observes the scene and outputs motion targets. Unlike other direct policies, call outputs an ordered sequence of absolute 6-DoF keyposes, placed with metric 3D measurements, that can span whole primitive. Sparse action representations. Sparsity itself is not new. Keyframe policies predict the next gripper pose rather than dense trajectory [21, 23, 24, 30, 33, 54], and bimanual policies condition on keyposes or skills [65, 67, 75]. These methods learn from task demonstrations, and they extract keyframes with heuristics such as gripper state changes and near-zero joint velocities [30, 54], implicitly assuming that few poses suffice; our analysis quantifies how many are needed per primitive and where this assumption fails. VLMbased methods such as VoxPoser [28], ReKep [29], and PIVOT [47] are also training-free, but the model typically produces object-centric keypoints, constraints or value maps once, and separate optimizer turns them into motion. In SOLVE, the model itself writes end-effector keyposes at every call (hence keypose rather than keypoint). 3. Method 3.1. Setup All experiments share the agent code, tools and executor; only the robots constants change (kinematic model, camera calibration, robot description in the prompt). We use only RGB observations, follow the official evaluation protocol, and report success rate (SR) and partial-credit score. RoboLab. RoboLab [63] comprises 120 tasks on Franka; we use its external and wrist RGB views and follow the official protocol, without guides. Real robot. Ablations Table 5 adds the components of SOLVE one at time to GPT-6 Astra (RoboProbe) [69]. Sparse keyposes. Replacing its step-wise end-effector actions with sparse keypose sequences, run by our executor, while still estimating targets from the RGB images, raises the average success rate from 22.9 to 49.5%. It gains most on Memory (38.7 to 92.5%), Long-Horizon (8.2 to 37.5%) and Precision (4.0 to 32.5%), where the step-by-step baseline runs out of steps before finishing. 3D queries. Measuring targets with query points raises it to 62.2% at about the same cost, mostly where centimeter matters: Precision rises from 32.5 to 60.0% and standard Generalization from 40.0 to 56.7%. Offline, 7 Figure 5. Keyposes written by SOLVE vs. keyposes demonstration needs, for the 34 RoboDojo tasks with demonstrations. Figure 6. Keyposes per call. (a) Success rate and (b) model calls per episode against the keyposes allowed per move eef call. on 1,182 queries of the Precision tasks with simulator depth as reference, intersecting pixels ray with the table errs by 51.6 mm (median) and object silhouettes by 20.0 mm, while epipolar matching errs by 4.6 mm on the 37% of pixels it accepts; on holes, where silhouettes fail, it is about ten times more accurate (2.8 vs. 36.4 mm on deposit coin). Online, triangulation and the Depth Anything 3 fallback raise the share of successful episodes from 55.5% with silhouettes alone to 59.8%, on par with simulator depth. Experience notes. Merged notes raise the average to 68.3% at no extra cost, mainly on Open (+15.0), Precision (+12.5) and Long-Horizon (+6.2). Raw notes add only 3 points in two independent writing runs, and their gains depend on what each run writes; notes that urge more verification make the agent run out of steps or give up. Merging three runs into at most five bounded rules per task removes such losses; on RoboLab, self-evolved notes likewise raise success from 79.8 to 84.5% (Tab. 3). 4.4. Analysis Keyposes. Figure 5 compares the keyposes SOLVE writes per episode with those teleoperated demonstration of the task needs. The two counts agree closely: medians of 39.5 vs. 40.3 per task, rank correlation of 0.90 over 34 tasks. This is not merely because both grow with the number of objects: with the demonstrations grasps and releases held fixed, the partial rank correlation remains 0.69. 8 Figure 7. Evolving the notes over more rounds. Bold: SR per five rounds; dashed and dotted: our merged rules and no notes. Keyposes per call. We cap move eef call at one, three or five keyposes and change nothing else  (Fig. 6)  . Success is unchanged (69.8, 67.8 and 68.2%), but model calls per episode fall from 56.6 to 36.2 and 33.7, 40% fewer. higher cap would save little more in simulation: even with five allowed, the agent sends one to three keyposes in 89% of its calls and five in only 3%, as it often splits primitive across calls to look in between. Drawing needs many more: on the real robot, cap of 30 lets the agent draw portraits 305 keyposes in 15 move eef calls instead of at least 61, each saving seconds of model latency. Evolving over more rounds. We let the agent keep evolving its notes for 20 rounds, each running one new layout per RoboDojo task  (Fig. 7)  . Starting from 59.8% without notes, success reaches 66.0, 68.4, 69.0 and 65.6% after 5, 10, 15 and 20 rounds: it peaks near our frozen merged rules (68.3%) and then declines. It is also unstable: single rounds swing between 57.1% and 76.2%, while three runs with the frozen merged rules average 68.6%. The notes explain both: as they fill up, the agent stops adding and rewrites them around the latest episode, so that most notes end up describing one particular episode and earlier lessons are overwritten. Merging avoids this: it keeps only layout-free lessons that recur across independent runs and freezes them, reaching the peak from the start and holding it across runs. 5. Conclusion An LLM agent does not need dense, step-by-step control to manipulate. Teleoperated demonstrations compress to few keyposes per grasp or release, and SOLVE lets multimodal LLM agent write such keyposes directly, grounds them with sparse metric queries, and refines them with notes from its own rollouts, without training. SOLVE reaches 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, ahead of every leaderboard entry, at $1.7 per episode, and 88% over 16 zero-shot real-world tasks. Sparse, ordered keyposes are an effective and economical interface between LLMs and robot control. Limitations. Some real tasks require force or continuous feedback that keyposes cannot provide, and each model call takes seconds; next step is to combine keyposes with learned low-level policy for contact-rich segments.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: A. Overview Setting Value This supplementary material complements the main paper in five parts. Implementation details (Sec. B): the settings of the agent loop, the executor, the query tool and the experience notes. Additional analyses (Sec. C): how far demonstrations compress into keyposes, how accurately query pixels are measured by epipolar matching and its fallbacks, what happens when notes keep evolving over many more rounds, and why the remaining RoboDojo episodes fail. Prompts (Sec. D): the system prompt, the tool descriptions, the prompts that write, merge and generalize experience notes, and the prompt that writes task guides. More experiments (Sec. E): controlled comparisons on public RoboDojo subset (task inputs, reasoning effort and another model), the real-robot experiment in detail, and RoboTwin 2.0 as third simulated benchmark. Visualizations (Sec. F): keyframes of one episode of every real-robot task and of ten solved tasks of each simulated benchmark. The supplementary archive also contains an offline webpage (open index.html in browser) with videos of the realrobot episodes and of RoboDojo, RoboLab and RoboTwin rollouts. B. Implementation details Table 6 lists the settings of SOLVE; they are the same for every task and, except where noted, every benchmark. Agent loop. The agent is called through an OpenAIcompatible Responses API and must answer every turn with exactly one tool call; if call has invalid arguments, such as sequence of more than five keyposes, it is rejected with an explanation and the agent is prompted again. Each call carries note, one or two sentences on what the agent sees and why it acts, which is logged and kept in the history (Sec. E.2.1 quotes such notes). Only the latest two observations keep their images (Sec. 3.1); older images are replaced by placeholders. Feedback. After move eef call, the next observation contains the current camera images, each arms grasp-point pose and gripper opening, and the feedback em: for each arm, the distance from each commanded keypose; any slip (which stops that arm and skips its remaining keyposes) or fully closed grasp (which is reported without stopping); the keypose at which the planner refused sequence, if any; and the remaining environment steps. move that would take Agent Model, effort Model calls per episode Tool calls per model call Images kept Executor Keyposes per call nmax Planned segment Joint speed Ramp Settling tolerance Slip detection Query tool Pixels per call Depth hypotheses Matching window Second views Depth estimation scale Experience Raw notes per set Writing Task rules Etask General rules Egen GPT-6.1 Sol / GPT-6 Astra, xhigh 600 (150 on RoboTwin) exactly one latest 2 observations 5 (30 for drawing on the real robot) 5 cm and 20 0.1 rad per step (25 Hz) 2 steps by default, 012 0.002 / 0.01 rad (contact / free) held 3 mm, then closed 32 0.5 to 36 cm above table, step 1.5 mm 1515, weighted NCC other cameras, 6 past wrist frames median over 2,000 table pixels 10, 110 words, 2 frames = 3 sets = 5 rollouts = 5 at most, 70 words, 2 rollouts 8, 60 words, 5 tasks Table 6. Writing and evaluation layouts. On both RoboDojo and RoboLab, experience notes are written only on layouts that differ from the evaluation layouts, then merged and frozen before evaluation, so no evaluation layout is seen while writing notes. The first rollout on RoboLab (Sec. 4.2) is the evaluation without notes; the self-evolved notes are written on other layouts and then used to evaluate the same evaluation layouts again. Evaluation protocols of the main tables. The rows of Tab. 1 follow two protocols. The row with GPT-6 Astra is the official evaluation run by the RoboDojo team on seed 3, hidden seed chosen by the organizers, with 50 episodes per task and 2,100 in all; the rows with GPT-6.1 Sol are the mean of two independent runs on seeds 0 and 1, five episodes per task. As on the leaderboard, Average first averages Generalization over its standard and randomized splits, then averages the result with the other four dimensions. Table 5 keeps only the standard Generalization split and averages its five columns, so the same configuration has slightly different averages in the two tables: 22.5 vs. 22.9% for GPT-6 Astra (RoboProbe), 61.5 vs. 62.2% for SOLVE 1 without notes, and 68.0 vs. 68.3% with the frozen merged rules. The single-factor analyses, namely the online comparison of depth sources (Sec. 4.3), Fig. 6 and the evaluations of Fig. 7, use single runs on seed 0 and report the share of its 209 standard episodes that succeed: five layouts for each of the 42 tasks, less one layout of imitate sorting sequence that the simulator marks unstable and never starts (Sec. E.1). Table 3 runs five episodes for each of the 120 tasks, 600 in all. Compute and cost. Each episode runs on one GPU, which serves the motion planner and Depth Anything 3; the model is called through its API. Cost is computed from the logged token usage at the models list price, including prompt-cache discounts. C. Additional analyses C.1. Keypose compression of demonstrations This section details the analysis of Sec. 3.2. Data. RoboDojo provides 100 teleoperated demonstrations for each of its 34 tasks with demonstrations, recorded at 25 Hz on two ARX-X5 arms; we convert each arm to the grasp point used by move eef, count the keyposes of both arms together, and skip an arm that moves less than 2 cm and 5. For DROID [34] we take all 57,639 successful episodes (15 Hz, Franka with Robotiq 2F-85) and drop those that move less than 2 cm and 5 or last under one second, leaving 57,534 episodes and 18.7M frames, without subsampling. We use DROIDs recorded end-effector pose, detect gripper events with hysteresis (closed above 0.4, open below 0.2, ignoring flips shorter than three frames), and smooth positions over about 0.2 before measuring path lengths, which changes the shares of long segments by less than 0.3 points. Robustness. On RoboDojo, every task has at least 80% of its travel on straight segments longer than 5 cm, the lowest being push (80.2%) and pour liquid into cup (80.4%). The 13,144 failed DROID episodes compress similarly: 88.9% of their travel lies on long segments, against 91.3% for successes. Moving DROIDs recorded pose 15 cm along the tool axis, in case it is the flange rather than the fingertips, raises the median keyposes per episode from 13 to 15 and leaves the share at 91.2%. The analysis measures geometric compressibility only: neither the DROID nor the RoboDojo demonstrations record the states of the objects, so the compressed trajectories cannot be replayed to measure their success. C.2. Epipolar matching of query pixels query points must return the 3D point of the pixel the agent chose, often the center of hole or point on rim, from cameras that differ greatly in direction and scale. We compare our epipolar matching (Sec. 3.3) with the alternatives offline, on pixels that the agent actually queried, using as reference the 3D point measured on simulator depth for the same pixel. Implementation. Depth hypotheses lie on the query ray from 5 mm below to 36 cm above the table, 1.5 mm apart. At each one, the 1515 gray-level window around the query pixel is warped into the second view through horizontal plane or plane facing the query camera, whichever matches better, and compared by normalized cross-correlation with Gaussian weights, so that the pixels nearest the query decide. match is accepted if its score is high, if it stands out from the best score elsewhere on the ray, sr, by the ratio ρ = (1 sr)/(1 s), which rejects repeated structures, and if the window has texture (a gray-level spread of at least 4). We require 0.85 and ρ 1.5 for the current cameras and the previous observation, and 0.9 and ρ 2 for older wrist frames (up to six observations back), since objects may have moved; second view must be at least 2 cm or 8 away from the query camera. Why not feature matching. Triangulating from feature matches between two views is natural alternative, but it suits our queries poorly: the head and wrist cameras see the scene from very different directions and at very different scales, so local features often fail to match between them, and the pixel the agent queries, such as the center of hole, need not carry matchable feature at all, so its depth would have to be borrowed from matches nearby. Our epipolar matching instead searches along the ray of the queried pixel itself and warps the window by the plane-induced homography, which absorbs the differences in viewpoint and scale. Where it answers, it is accurate to millimeters. On all 1,182 query pixels of the Precision tasks (Tab. 7), epipolar matching answers 37% of the pixels, using the other cameras and the wrist frames of the last six observations, at median error of 4.6 mm; two thirds of its answers lie within 1 cm. This is about four times more accurate than measuring object silhouettes (20.0 mm) and ten times more than intersecting the pixels ray with the table (51.6 mm). The gap is largest on holes, where silhouette has no surface to measure: 2.8 vs. 36.4 mm on deposit coin. Past wrist frames raise the coverage from 24% to 37% at no loss of accuracy, since moving wrist camera provides new baselines for free. Where it does not, the tool falls back and says so. Pixels on textureless, slanted or specular surfaces have no reliable match; there the tool reads the depth estimated by Depth Anything 3, accurate to about centimeter, or the table plane, and tags each answer with its source. The agent therefore gets an answer for every pixel and knows which ones to trust to millimeters: the full chain answers all 1,182 pixels, not only the 37% that epipolar matching accepts, at median error of 5.4 mm, close to that of epipolar matching alone, 2 Method Coverage Median 1 cm Ray table plane Object silhouettes Epipolar, current views Epipolar, + past wrists 100% 97% 24% 37% 51.6 mm 20.0 mm 4.8 mm 4.6 mm Ours (epipolar, DA3, table) 100% 5.4 mm 10% 36% 68% 66% 64% Table 7. Offline accuracy of 3D queries on 1,182 query pixels of the Precision tasks, against the 3D point measured on simulator depth: share of pixels answered, median error and share within 1 cm. at every call; the last four are used offline, once per rollout or per task. On other robots only the robot description in the prompt changes (Sec. 4.1). Three principles recur across them. Measure, do not guess: every target is placed from query points on distinctive pixels, and each reading comes with its source. Steps are scarce: the prompts name the step budget, ask for final poses rather than small increments, and require every check or retry the agent or its notes add to be bounded. General, not layout-specific: guides tag what holds in any layout, and notes and rules state situations and actions without coordinates. and puts 64% of them within 1 cm, against 36% for object silhouettes and 10% for the table plane (Tab. 7). E. More experiments C.3. Evolving notes over more rounds In the experiment of Fig. 7, the agent keeps evolving its notes over 20 additional rounds instead of merging and freezing them (Sec. 4.4), using layouts that differ from the evaluation layouts. The resulting notes explain why performance stops improving and fluctuates: each task keeps at most ten notes, and once full, the agent mostly overwrites existing notes rather than adding new ones, replacing general lessons with accounts of the latest episode. For example, play stacking toy note on grasping square pieces between occupied pegs ends up reading This success placed all three squares between tall ring stack and blue block. . . . Merging keeps only lessons that several independent rollouts support, stated without layout details, and freezing stops the latest episode from rewriting them, which is why SOLVE merges and freezes its notes. C.4. Failure analysis on RoboDojo We classify every failed episode of our runs with notes on layouts 04 of seed 0, standard and randomized variants (269 evaluated episodes per model), by its primary cause and by how it ended  (Fig. 8)  . The cause is labeled by an LLM from evidence extracted from the trace: grasp-monitor events, planner refusals, the sources of the queried points, and the reason and hindsight that the agent states when it gives up. Contact, not perception. With either model, two causes account for more than three quarters of the failures: grasp that slips or closes empty, and placement or alignment that is off, such as pen released on the rim of its holder or keyboard pushed past its frame. No failure is primarily due to wrong 3D measurement, and none to memory: where the agent fails, it usually knows where things are and what remains to be done, but cannot hold or seat them. D. Prompts Table 8 summarizes the prompts of SOLVE on RoboDojo, which are written in English. The agent reads the first three E.1. Controlled comparisons on public subset To separate the factors behind SOLVEs results, we rerun it with one factor changed at time on fixed subset: the 50 RoboDojo episodes whose step-wise GPT-6 Astra Direct runs are public [56], ten tasks on seed 0 (41 standard and 9 randomized episodes). One of them, layout 4 of imitate sorting sequence, never starts because the simulator marks it unstable, so every configuration is evaluated on the same 49 episodes. Unless stated otherwise, the configuration is that of the paper: GPT-6.1 Sol at effort xhigh, at most five keyposes per call, task guides, and the frozen merged rules, task and general, of every task. All configurations of Tab. 9 run in the same batch, including the default SOLVE configuration, and are compared with it episode by episode (exact McNemar test). The subset leans toward Long-Horizon (20 of 50 episodes) and has one task each from Precision, Memory and Open. With 49 episodes, only large differences can be resolved: two configurations must differ by about ten episodes to be statistically distinguishable. Guides and notes. Removing either the guide or the notes costs six episodes (33 to 27), and removing both costs 14 (p = 0.009). The two inputs are thus partly interchangeable: without notes, the guide adds 8 episodes (19 to 27), and without the guide, the notes add 8 as well, while together they add 14. Both convey how to approach the task, the guide from demonstration and the notes from the agents own rollouts, so either one recovers much of what the other provides. Without either, SOLVE still solves 19 of 49 episodes with GPT-6.1 Sol, compared with 13 of 50 for the step-wise GPT-6 Astra Direct with the stronger GPT-6 Astra. Reasoning effort. Lowering GPT-6.1 Sols effort from xhigh to high or medium lowers the cost per episode by 8% and 22%, while success changes only within the noise of 49 episodes. Another model. With the same prompt, tools, guides and notes, Gemini 4 Argon (at high, the highest effort its endpoint accepts) solves 30 of 49 episodes, close to GPT-6.1 Sol and with fewer calls (29.4), so SOLVE works with another frontier model without any change. 3 Figure 8. Where RoboDojo failures come from. Every failed episode of our runs with notes on layouts 04 of seed 0, including the randomized variants (269 episodes per model), flows from its dimension (left) to its primary cause (middle) and to how it ended (right); band widths are numbers of episodes, colored by cause. No failure is primarily attributed to wrong 3D measurement or to memory. E.2. Real robot Setup. The setup follows Sec. 4.1: UR12e with Robotiq 2F-85; wrist Orbbec Gemini 335Lg and fixed thirdperson Intel RealSense; the same agent, tools and executor as on RoboDojo; wrist stereo depth and cross-camera triangulation; and no pre-collected demonstrations, guides, notes or task-specific code. For drawing, the cap nmax is raised from five to 30 keyposes per move eef call, which long strokes need; the portrait instruction states this cap explicitly. Each task is given as one natural-language instruction. When task involves person, the agent lets the person act with wait and sees the frames recorded meanwhile. Success is verified by person against fixed criterion per task, such as stable four-level stack, fully seated workpiece or five marks in row, and confirmed on the final camera frames; 75 of the 85 episodes succeed (Tab. 4). Whether task ran with GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra was assigned randomly before the experiment and kept fixed; the prompt was also finalized before any real-robot run and was never tuned on these tasks. We also tried the GPT-6 Astra (RoboProbe) baseline [69] once per task; single episode usually took more than 30 minutes at high API cost, and none succeeded, so we did not scale it up or report it in Tab. 4. Every episode is judged for success; per-episode statistics (model calls, keyposes, queried pixels and time) in Tab. 4 and Tab. 10 are computed over the episodes with full logs, one or more per task. Table 10 details each of the 16 tasks, and Sec. shows one successful episode per task. 3D queries on the real robot. queried pixel takes the FoundationStereo [58] depth of the wrist cameras infrared pair around it, then cross-camera triangulation between the wrist and third-person cameras where that depth is missing, and falls back to the table plane, each answer tagged with its source and warned when noisy. The wrist camera is calibrated by hand-eye calibration (TsaiLenz) on chessboard, and the third-person cameras pose is calibrated from chessboards viewed jointly by both cameras. The agent sets the keypose density. Keyposes per move eef call range from 1.6 for insertion, where the agent moves in short sequences and looks after each, to 20.3 for the portrait (Tab. 10). grasp and place takes three or four keyposes, sent in sequences of 2.32.6 on the Long-Horizon tasks, close to RoboDojo, while drawing grows with the length of the strokes: 45 keyposes for house, 125 for the rocket and 305 for the portrait. Model calls vary far less, from 11 to 33 per episode, so the cost of an episode is set by how often the agent needs to look, not by how much it draws. Failures. The ten failures fall on shirt folding (4 of 10), precision (3 of 10) and open tasks (3 of 25). Most concern contact: an insertion releases before the pegs are seated, or shirt slides along with the gripper during one-arm fold. The others concern the clearance of the robots own body: lowering pen grasped near its tip would have brought the wrist camera into collision with the table, and the robot stopped before contact; this is also why the portrait and Gomoku instructions, written before the experiment like all others, ask to grasp the pen near its end. As on RoboDojo, these call for force or tactile feedback at contact and collision check of the whole arm and camera before sequence is sent. Time. logged episode takes 6.6 minutes on average; model call takes median of 11.7 and executing its keypose sequence 6.1 s, so inference, not motion, sets the pace, which confines SOLVE to quasi-static scenes (Sec. 5).
